Hi all,

Today on the JobQueue call, we discussed moving from using the XArray as storage for jobs in the JobQueue to having ListArcs instead.

So as we discussed on the call, my main worry is that, by switching to lists, we may eventually reintroduce problems that @Sami Tolvanen has already fixed in the XArray JQ implementation. There was a lot of work there to make sure that CTS passes without splats and we remain as performant as Panthor in benchmarks. This work will probably transfer over to Nova, Asahi and others. By doing away with the core idea that the queue is a pipeline of jobs in different stages, whose position is tracked via the index allocated by the XArray, this may break in ways we will have to rediscover.

If I understand correctly, there are issues with the current XArray, my proposal is that we fix them. Subsequently, my proposal is that we later switch to the Rust XArray that @Daniel Gomez and @Andreas Hindborg are working on, as that will probably not have these issues from the start if we deliberately try to avoid them.

In any case, although I strongly prefer keeping the XArray design, I understand this may not be the consensus, which is completely understandable in upstream work. I therefore propose we use this topic to collectively discuss some of the issues while @Philipp Stanner iterates on the ListArc code.
cc @Deborah Brouwer @Danilo Krummrich @Alice Ryhl @Gary Guo

@Andreas Hindborg The issue Daniel is referring to is that XArray does not free internal nodes if the index is ever-increasing, which is the case for Tyr's JobQueue draft.

Another issue is that XArray runs into massively deep trees for large indices, even if you have few entries. Matthew Wilcox told me that for something approaching u32::max that will be like 11 pointer indirections for each ID lookup. That's also not cool in a job submission path :eyes:

IDK if the C xarray issue can be solved, because the internal nodes not being freed seems to be by-design. So I would expect that the C Xarray pushes back a gainst freeing those nodes.

That would have to be determined by someone who hypothetically tries to make this change in C

@Philipp Stanner @Daniel Almeida, how many jobs can you have at once? In the roadmap we shared at Kangrejos, I briefly mentioned about the shrink/expand tree. @Andreas Hindborg I wonder if we can have some sort of ring buffer node for this shrink/expand situations where we keep the tree in "shrink" mode as long as we do not have more than N entries.

@Daniel Gomez Like we discussed, my proposal is that you take in the initial number of slots as an argument, and that you offer a reserve()-like API where this can be grown in the future if needed. Thus, if for some reason the initial value is not enough, it can be grown by the driver at a future point when it's safe to do so (i.e.: outside of the dma signaling path).

I like this ring buffer design you propose, so long as it does not break the monotonically increasing nature of the indices.

@Philipp Stanner I think you probably need two locks, see https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/panfrost/linux/-/blob/tyr-dev/rust/kernel/drm/job_queue.rs?ref_type=heads#L75 and https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/panfrost/linux/-/blob/tyr-dev/rust/kernel/drm/job_queue.rs?ref_type=heads#L79, otherwise you will probably reintroduce this deadlock:

At the top of each tick(), the pipeline drains entries from
submitted_start..submitted_end into deps_range. This allows the queue to accept
more submissions while the rest of the queue is locked due to a tick being in
progress. Ignoring this separation may cause a deadlock because the driver's
submit() path may take driver locks and then wait on the state mutex held by
tick(), while tick() waits on said driver locks during handler.submit().

The current design solves this lock ordering problem by splitting submit() and
tick() state into two separate locks: inbox for the submission path, and state
for the tick path. The inbox mutex is only held briefly at the top of tick() to
drain new submissions, while the rest of the tick logic (including calls to the
driver's submit()) happens under the state mutex, which is never touched by
submit().
@Daniel Almeida yes, I forgot it was you that suggested that. Yes, ring buffer honoring that constraint.

Maybe we should discuss the lock issue in a separate thread?
I suggest focussing on xarray vs list for now

@Philipp Stanner the Rust xarray takes care of the entries when slots are dropped. I wonder if it makes sense to leverage this ring-buffer design idea to take care the nodes we leave behind to automatically drop them together with their entries.

The issue Daniel is referring to is that XArray does not free internal nodes if the index is ever-increasing, which is the case for Tyr's JobQueue draft.

OOC, is this a property of the C API, or something we encoded in the rust abstraction wrapping around it? It seemed to me that xa_erase() would remove internal nodes as you start collecting low indices. Seems that if it wasn't true, the "The XArray is optimised for small indices, but still has good performance with large indices." in https://docs.kernel.org/core-api/xarray.html wouldn't hold.

Another issue is that XArray runs into massively deep trees for large indices, even if you have few entries. Matthew Wilcox told me that for something approaching u32::max that will be like 11 pointer indirections for each ID lookup. That's also not cool in a job submission path :grinning_face_with_smiling_eyes:

Again, that goes against this statement "The XArray implementation is efficient when the indices used are densely clustered;" in the same spec.

My understanding was that xa_array is efficient as long as live indices do not exhibit holes, and the range of live indices is relatively small

I wonder if the 11 indirections Matthew mentioned is for the case where index 0 and index ULONG_MAX are populated, which might not really happen in our case (job indices is a sliding window, where indices are retired from bottom to top)

OOC, is this a property of the C API

That's a on the C xarray

"The XArray implementation is efficient when the indices used are densely clustered;" in the same spec.

Once you reached the end leaves. For accessing arbitrarily large indices, you will have to go through the depth of the internal nodes.

Let's wait for @Andreas Hindborg , he can edcuate us on that
BTW, isn't it exactly what https://elixir.bootlin.com/linux/v7.2.5/source/lib/test_xarray.c#L324 tests?
I think the issue is that it does not free internal nodes. The leave nodes can get merged / shrink

I wonder if the 11 indirections Matthew mentioned is for the case where index 0 and index ULONG_MAX are populated, which might not really happen in our case (job indices is a sliding window, where indices are retired from bottom to top)

Scratch that, it will happen when you approach ULONG_MAX, because it wraps around and starts populating entries from zero while entries at the end of the xarray are still alive, but this is just a transient state

Philipp Stanner said in #DRM > JobQueue discussion:

Andreas Hindborg The issue Daniel is referring to is that XArray does not free internal nodes if the index is ever-increasing, which is the case for Tyr's JobQueue draft.

Another issue is that XArray runs into massively deep trees for large indices, even if you have few entries. Matthew Wilcox told me that for something approaching u32::max that will be like 11 pointer indirections for each ID lookup. That's also not cool in a job submission path :eyes:

IDK if the C xarray issue can be solved, because the internal nodes not being freed seems to be by-design. So I would expect that the C Xarray pushes back a gainst freeing those nodes.

That would have to be determined by someone who hypothetically tries to make this change in C

Did you double check this? I was looking over the xarray C code last week with @Daniel Gomez and we found code that will delete nodes and compact the tree. Basically when you delete nodes by storing NULL to their location, they are deleted and freed.
I'm not fully on top of this, so please check the code path.

Daniel Almeida said:

Daniel Gomez Like we discussed, my proposal is that you take in the initial number of slots as an argument, and that you offer a reserve()-like API where this can be grown in the future if needed. Thus, if for some reason the initial value is not enough, it can be grown by the driver at a future point when it's safe to do so (i.e.: outside of the dma signaling path).

I like this ring buffer design you propose, so long as it does not break the monotonically increasing nature of the indices.

I think we have room for a growable ring buffer data structure. It should be managable. I have a statically sized one on list.

Philipp Stanner said:

I think the issue is that it does not free internal nodes. The leave nodes can get merged / shrink

The test I pointed to checks the root node, so I don't know where the internal nodes would be if that was the case, unless they are purely and simply leaked...
Unless there's some sideband storage I missed...

As for u32::max being the max number of queued job, I guess we might want to make that smaller, 4billion of pending jobs sounds unrealistic to me, and we probably want some throttling to happen before that (will happen naturally because of lack of memory anyway)

If you delete an entry it is accounted for here and when update_node is called after the operation here, if any node was deleted, the node is unlinked and freed if empty here before return. If the delete operation changes the refcount on the root, the tree shrinker is invoked.

So you will not have any empty nodes inside the tree dangling.

But the tree shrinking is an optimization that removes tree levels when the indicies in the tree are small. So when your moving id range moves to the upper part of the tree, you get full depth, which is 6 levels in the normal server configuration, if I remember correctly.

@Philipp Stanner I know I told you otherwise at an earlier occation. Turns out we were reading the code wrong. I did a deep dive with @Daniel Gomez before Kangrejos, and we learned that we were mistaken.
